claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disease with motor and non-motor symptoms, including constipation.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disease with motor and non-motor symptoms, including constipation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PD symptoms presented in the abstract.

claim: α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of intracellular Ca2+ concentration probably contribute to the pathogenesis of PD.
source: Besides α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of intracellular Ca2+ concentration probably contribute to the pathogenesis of PD.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents current scientific understanding.

claim: Submucous neurons were not affected in PD patients.
source: We found that submucous neurons were not affected in PD patients, which suggests that these neurons are not involved in the pathogenesis or the gastrointestinal symptoms of PD.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the calcium imaging and mitochondrial imaging data presented in the results section.

claim: Submucous neurons are not involved in the pathogenesis or the gastrointestinal symptoms of PD.
source: We found that submucous neurons were not affected in PD patients, which suggests that these neurons are not involved in the pathogenesis or the gastrointestinal symptoms of PD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that submucous neurons were not affected.

claim: This study provides for the first time functional information on live neurons in PD patients.
source: Our study provides for the first time functional information on live neurons in PD patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: PD is the most prevalent neurodegenerative movement disorder.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the most prevalent neurodegenerative movement disorder.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PD epidemiology.

claim: The defining pathological features of PD are the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra (SN) and the intraneuronal presence of α-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites).
source: The defining pathological features of PD are the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra (SN) and the intraneuronal presence of α-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites) (Lees et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lees et al., 2009.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of calcium homeostasis are thought to play a crucial role in PD pathogenesis.
source: Although the pathogenic mechanisms underlying PD are not understood in detail, mitochondrial dysfunction and dysregulation of calcium homeostasis are thought to play a crucial role (Exner et al., 2012; Surmeier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Exner et al., 2012 and Surmeier et al., 2013.

claim: PD patients can develop a variety of disabling non-motor symptoms including psychosis, depression, hyposmia, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder and constipation.
source: Besides the well-known motor problems, PD patients can develop a variety of disabling non-motor symptoms (Lees et al., 2009), like psychosis, depression, hyposmia, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder and constipation, some of which can even occur prior to the first motor manifestations (Goldman and Postuma, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lees et al., 2009 and Goldman and Postuma, 2014.

claim: Some non-motor symptoms of PD can occur prior to the first motor manifestations.
source: Besides the well-known motor problems, PD patients can develop a variety of disabling non-motor symptoms (Lees et al., 2009), like psychosis, depression, hyposmia, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder and constipation, some of which can even occur prior to the first motor manifestations (Goldman and Postuma, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldman and Postuma, 2014.

claim: Several studies have reported the presence of α-synuclein aggregates in the enteric nervous system (ENS) in fixed biopsy material or postmortem tissue from PD patients.
source: Several studies have reported the presence of α-synuclein aggregates in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which controls GI function, in fixed biopsy material or postmortem tissue from PD patients (Lebouvier et al., 2008; Shannon et al., 2012a; Pouclet et al., 2012a; Derkinderen et al., 2011) suggesting that the ENS is directly affected by the disease process.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Lebouvier et al., 2008; Shannon et al., 2012a; Pouclet et al., 2012a; Derkinderen et al., 2011.

claim: The presence of α-synuclein aggregates in the ENS suggests that the ENS is directly affected by the disease process.
source: Several studies have reported the presence of α-synuclein aggregates in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which controls GI function, in fixed biopsy material or postmortem tissue from PD patients (Lebouvier et al., 2008; Shannon et al., 2012a; Pouclet et al., 2012a; Derkinderen et al., 2011) suggesting that the ENS is directly affected by the disease process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of α-synuclein aggregates in the ENS.

claim: According to the Braak hypothesis, an ingested pathogenic agent would enter nerve fibers in the GI tract and initiate α-synuclein misfolding, which would then propagate in a prion-like fashion along the axons up to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the lower brainstem.
source: According to this theory, an ingested pathogenic agent would enter nerve fibers in the GI tract and initiate α-synuclein misfolding, which would then propagate in a prion-like fashion along the axons up to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the lower brainstem (Braak et al., 2006; Hawkes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis supported by citations to Braak et al., 2006 and Hawkes et al., 2007.

claim: More recent studies have shown similar patterns of α-synuclein immunoreactivity in the ENS in a high percentage of neurologically unimpaired controls.
source: Nevertheless, more recent studies have shown similar patterns of α-synuclein immunoreactivity in the ENS in a high percentage of neurologically unimpaired controls (Visanji et al., 2014; Gold et al., 2013; Gray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Visanji et al., 2014; Gold et al., 2013; Gray et al., 2014.

claim: Not a single report has investigated the functionality of enteric neurons in PD patients prior to this study.
source: So far, not a single report has investigated the functionality of enteric neurons in PD patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on literature review.

claim: 15 couples were recruited, each consisting of a PD patient and his or her healthy partner.
source: We recruited 15 couples, each consisting of a PD patient and his or her healthy partner.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Pairwise recruitment allowed within-pair comparisons to better control for variability in diet, lifestyle and other environmental factors.
source: This pairwise recruitment allowed within-pair comparisons to better control for variability in diet, lifestyle and other environmental factors.
evidence: This is a rationale for the study design approach.

claim: The majority of PD participants were male.
source: As in most clinical PD studies, the majority of PD participants were male.
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the study population.

claim: PD patients and controls were age-matched.
source: PD patients and controls were age-matched and disease duration ranged from 2 to 17 years.
evidence: This is a description of the study population matching.

claim: Disease duration ranged from 2 to 17 years in PD patients.
source: PD patients and controls were age-matched and disease duration ranged from 2 to 17 years.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: All PD patients were under treatment with oral dopaminergic medication.
source: All PD patients were under treatment with oral dopaminergic medication.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: None of the PD patients were treated with apomorphine, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel or deep brain stimulation.
source: None were treated with apomorphine, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel or deep brain stimulation.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: Three PD patients had levodopa-induced dyskinesias.
source: Three patients had levodopa-induced dyskinesias, five had early morning dystonia and two had daytime motor fluctuations.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: Five PD patients had early morning dystonia.
source: Three patients had levodopa-induced dyskinesias, five had early morning dystonia and two had daytime motor fluctuations.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: Two PD patients had daytime motor fluctuations.
source: Three patients had levodopa-induced dyskinesias, five had early morning dystonia and two had daytime motor fluctuations.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: Six of the 15 PD patients had disease onset under the age of 46 years.
source: Six of the 15 patients had disease onset under the age of 46 years.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the PD patient population.

claim: Genetic analysis of the PARK2 gene was performed in 5 of the 6 patients with young-onset PD, but no mutations were found.
source: Genetic analysis of the PARK2 gene was performed in 5 of these 6 patients, but no mutations were found.
evidence: This is a result of genetic testing performed on a subset of patients.

claim: PD patients had significantly more autonomic and GI symptoms than controls.
source: Interestingly, although presence of autonomic and GI symptoms was not an inclusion criterion, PD patients had significantly more autonomic and GI symptoms than controls (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing SCOPA total and SCOPA GI scores.

claim: In controls, 57.3 ± 29.5% of neurons displayed a transient change in Fluo-4 intensity upon depolarization with high K+.
source: In controls, 57.3 ± 29.5% of neurons displayed a transient change in Fluo-4 intensity (with maximum amplitude of 3.6 ± 2%, n = 15.6 ± 2.9 neurons per subject) upon depolarization with high K+.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: No significant difference was found in the percentage of high K+ responding neurons between PD patients (49.5 ± 28.7%) and controls (57.3 ± 29.5%).
source: No significant difference was found when compared to PD patients, where both the number of high K+ responding neurons (49.5 ± 28.7%, p=0.47) and the [Ca2+]i transient amplitudes (2.8 ± 3%, p=0.37, n = 11.9 ± 1.9 neurons per patient) were similar (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of calcium imaging data between groups, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The [Ca2+]i transient amplitudes were similar between PD patients (2.8 ± 3%) and controls (3.6 ± 2%).
source: No significant difference was found when compared to PD patients, where both the number of high K+ responding neurons (49.5 ± 28.7%, p=0.47) and the [Ca2+]i transient amplitudes (2.8 ± 3%, p=0.37, n = 11.9 ± 1.9 neurons per patient) were similar (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of calcium imaging data between groups, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentage of responding neurons and [Ca2+]i transient amplitudes in the PD group did not correlate with age, GI symptoms, disease duration or disease severity.
source: The percentage of responding neurons and [Ca2+]i transient amplitudes in the PD group did not correlate with age, GI symptoms (as measured by the Scale for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease for Autonomic Symptoms (SCOPA-AUT), disease duration or disease severity (as assessed by Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) part III off medication (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Neither for DMPP nor for electrical stimulation were differences in percentages of responding neurons or response amplitudes found between PD patients and controls.
source: However, neither for DMPP nor for electrical stimulation, differences in percentages of responding neurons or response amplitudes were found (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result of calcium imaging experiments with different stimuli, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The TMRE signals at room temperature were similar in both PD patients and controls.
source: The TMRE signals at RT were similar in both groups (Figure 3B) and did not correlate with age, Gl symptoms, disease duration or severity of PD patients (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of mitochondrial imaging experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TMRE signals at room temperature did not correlate with age, GI symptoms, disease duration or severity of PD patients.
source: The TMRE signals at RT were similar in both groups (Figure 3B) and did not correlate with age, Gl symptoms, disease duration or severity of PD patients (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The intensity of the TMRE staining fluctuated substantially in both PD patients and controls, indicating that mitochondrial potentials were dynamically changing.
source: The intensity of the TMRE staining fluctuated substantially, indicating that both in PD patients and controls mitochondrial potentials were dynamically changing (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is an observation from mitochondrial imaging experiments shown in Figures 3C-D.

claim: TMRE intensity fluctuations were not significantly different between PD patients and controls.
source: Here again, TMRE intensity fluctuations were not significantly different between PD patients and controls (Figure 3E), without any correlations with the clinical characteristics of PD patients (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of mitochondrial imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: TMRE intensity fluctuations did not correlate with clinical characteristics of PD patients.
source: Here again, TMRE intensity fluctuations were not significantly different between PD patients and controls (Figure 3E), without any correlations with the clinical characteristics of PD patients (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The volumes of the outlined ganglia were not significantly different between PD patients and controls.
source: The volumes of the outlined ganglia were not significantly different between the 2 groups (data not shown), nor was the total mitochondrial volume inside the selection (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result of mitochondrial volume analysis.

claim: The total mitochondrial volume inside the ganglion selection was not significantly different between PD patients and controls.
source: The volumes of the outlined ganglia were not significantly different between the 2 groups (data not shown), nor was the total mitochondrial volume inside the selection (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result of mitochondrial volume analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mitochondrial volume did not significantly correlate with age, GI symptoms, disease duration or severity of PD patients.
source: The mitochondrial volume did not significantly correlate with age, GI symptoms, disease duration or severity of PD patients (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Mitochondrial density (number of mitochondria within the ganglion outline) was not significantly different between PD patients and controls.
source: In addition to total mitochondrial volume, we also analysed mitochondrial density (number of mitochondria within the ganglion outline). This parameter was again not significantly different between the two groups (Figure 4C) and did not correlate with clinical characteristics in the PD group (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of mitochondrial density analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mitochondrial density did not correlate with clinical characteristics in the PD group.
source: In addition to total mitochondrial volume, we also analysed mitochondrial density (number of mitochondria within the ganglion outline). This parameter was again not significantly different between the two groups (Figure 4C) and did not correlate with clinical characteristics in the PD group (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The average volume of individual mitochondria did not significantly differ between PD patients and controls.
source: Lastly, we compared average volume of individual mitochondria and, similarly to other mitochondrial parameters, this did not significantly differ between the two groups (Figure 4D), nor was it correlated with any of the clinical parameters (Supplementary file 3) (Video 4).
evidence: This is a result of mitochondrial volume analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average volume of individual mitochondria was not correlated with any of the clinical parameters in PD patients.
source: Lastly, we compared average volume of individual mitochondria and, similarly to other mitochondrial parameters, this did not significantly differ between the two groups (Figure 4D), nor was it correlated with any of the clinical parameters (Supplementary file 3) (Video 4).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The number of neurons per ganglion did not differ between PD patients and controls.
source: Finally, we counted the number of neurons per ganglion, total number of neurons per biopsy and number of ganglia per biopsy in both groups based on immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5A). None of these parameters differed between the two groups (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a result of immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The total number of neurons per biopsy did not differ between PD patients and controls.
source: Finally, we counted the number of neurons per ganglion, total number of neurons per biopsy and number of ganglia per biopsy in both groups based on immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5A). None of these parameters differed between the two groups (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a result of immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The number of ganglia per biopsy did not differ between PD patients and controls.
source: Finally, we counted the number of neurons per ganglion, total number of neurons per biopsy and number of ganglia per biopsy in both groups based on immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5A). None of these parameters differed between the two groups (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a result of immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No correlations were found between neuronal counts and age, GI symptoms, disease duration or disease severity of PD patients.
source: No correlations were found between these counts and age, GI symptoms, disease duration or disease severity of PD patients (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a result of correlation analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The α-synuclein staining patterns were indistinguishable between PD patients and controls.
source: We also tested whether α-synuclein aggregates were present in the samples using an antibody against α-synuclein. However, the staining patterns were indistinguishable between PD patients and controls (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a result of immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: GI symptoms in PD do not arise from disturbed submucous neuronal function.
source: Although GI symptoms were not an inclusion criterion for PD patients in this study, the PD patients had more GI symptoms than controls, in line with previous data (Fasano et al., 2015). Our finding of preserved neuronal functionality in these patients suggests that GI symptoms in PD do not arise from disturbed submucous neuronal function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of preserved neuronal functionality in PD patients with GI symptoms.

claim: GI symptoms in PD may possibly be caused by impaired function of neurons of the myenteric plexus.
source: Instead, GI symptoms may possibly be caused by impaired function of neurons of the myenteric plexus, the deeper nerve layer innervating the GI muscle.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the finding that submucous neurons are not affected.

claim: The submucous plexus predominantly controls secretion, whereas the myenteric plexus predominantly controls motility.
source: The submucous plexus predominantly controls secretion, whereas the myenteric plexus predominantly controls motility (Furness, 2006) and may thus be more involved in delayed gastric emptying and constipation in PD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ENS function supported by citation to Furness, 2006.

claim: The myenteric plexus may be more involved in delayed gastric emptying and constipation in PD.
source: The submucous plexus predominantly controls secretion, whereas the myenteric plexus predominantly controls motility (Furness, 2006) and may thus be more involved in delayed gastric emptying and constipation in PD.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the functional roles of different ENS layers.

claim: It is not possible to safely sample the myenteric plexus with routine endoscopic biopsies because of the risk of bleeding.
source: However, it is not possible to safely sample the myenteric plexus with routine endoscopic biopsies because of the risk of bleeding.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of endoscopic sampling.

claim: Another possible anatomic substrate for GI dysfunction in PD is the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the brainstem.
source: Another possible anatomic substrate for GI dysfunction in PD is the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the brainstem, which is heavily affected by PD pathology (Braak and Del Tredici, 2008) and innervates neurons of the myenteric plexus via vagal nerve connections.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citation to Braak and Del Tredici, 2008.

claim: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is heavily affected by PD pathology.
source: Another possible anatomic substrate for GI dysfunction in PD is the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the brainstem, which is heavily affected by PD pathology (Braak and Del Tredici, 2008) and innervates neurons of the myenteric plexus via vagal nerve connections.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Braak and Del Tredici, 2008.

claim: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus innervates neurons of the myenteric plexus via vagal nerve connections.
source: Another possible anatomic substrate for GI dysfunction in PD is the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the brainstem, which is heavily affected by PD pathology (Braak and Del Tredici, 2008) and innervates neurons of the myenteric plexus via vagal nerve connections.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Chronic oral ingestion of low-dose rotenone in mice was reported to trigger α-synuclein accumulation in ENS ganglia and subsequently in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve and substantia nigra.
source: Chronic oral ingestion of low-dose rotenone in mice was reported to trigger α-synuclein accumulation in ENS ganglia and subsequently in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve and substantia nigra, a sequence that was interrupted by vagotomy (Pan-Montojo et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan-Montojo et al., 2010, 2012.

claim: The sequence of α-synuclein accumulation from ENS to brain in rotenone-treated mice was interrupted by vagotomy.
source: Chronic oral ingestion of low-dose rotenone in mice was reported to trigger α-synuclein accumulation in ENS ganglia and subsequently in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve and substantia nigra, a sequence that was interrupted by vagotomy (Pan-Montojo et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan-Montojo et al., 2010, 2012.

claim: An epidemiological study reported that truncal vagotomy may be associated with a decreased risk of subsequent PD.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, an epidemiological study reported that truncal vagotomy may be associated with a decreased risk of subsequent PD (Tysnes et al., 2015), although this link is still controversial (Svensson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tysnes et al., 2015.

claim: The link between truncal vagotomy and decreased PD risk is still controversial.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, an epidemiological study reported that truncal vagotomy may be associated with a decreased risk of subsequent PD (Tysnes et al., 2015), although this link is still controversial (Svensson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Svensson et al., 2015.

claim: The data in living human neurons do not support the theory that an ingested pathogen would induce toxicity in myenteric neurons and vagal nerve fibres while preserving the functionality of submucous neurons.
source: Our data in living human neurons do not support this theory, as it seems unlikely that an ingested pathogen would induce toxicity in myenteric neurons and vagal nerve fibres while preserving the functionality of submucous neurons, which are located more closely to the gut lumen and whose fibres extend into the mucosa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study findings in the context of the Braak hypothesis.

claim: Submucous neurons are located more closely to the gut lumen than myenteric neurons and their fibres extend into the mucosa.
source: Our data in living human neurons do not support this theory, as it seems unlikely that an ingested pathogen would induce toxicity in myenteric neurons and vagal nerve fibres while preserving the functionality of submucous neurons, which are located more closely to the gut lumen and whose fibres extend into the mucosa.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: This study is the first to investigate the functionality of living enteric neurons of patients with PD or any other neurodegenerative disease at the cellular and subcellular level.
source: To our knowledge, this study is the first to investigate the functionality of living enteric neurons of patients with PD or any other neurodegenerative disease at the cellular and subcellular level.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: Many groups have modelled neurodegenerative diseases by generating neurons from patient fibroblasts via induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
source: Many groups have modelled neurodegenerative diseases by generating neurons from patient fibroblasts via induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (Ross and Akimov, 2014), but it is still uncertain how faithfully iPSC-derived neurons mimic the behavior of endogenous primary neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ross and Akimov, 2014.

claim: It is still uncertain how faithfully iPSC-derived neurons mimic the behavior of endogenous primary neurons.
source: Many groups have modelled neurodegenerative diseases by generating neurons from patient fibroblasts via induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (Ross and Akimov, 2014), but it is still uncertain how faithfully iPSC-derived neurons mimic the behavior of endogenous primary neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of iPSC models.

claim: Previous studies of the ENS in human PD have generally focused on patterns of α-synuclein immunoreactivity in fixed tissue.
source: Previous studies of the ENS in human PD have generally focused on patterns of α-synuclein immunoreactivity in fixed tissue.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research approaches.

claim: The well-known Braak staging of PD is exclusively based on detection of Lewy pathology but its link with neuronal function is still unclear.
source: It should be kept in mind that the well-known Braak staging of PD is also exclusively based on detection of Lewy pathology but its link with neuronal function is still unclear (Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Braak et al., 2003.

claim: The study had a prospective design.
source: Strengths of this study were its prospective design and the blinding of the investigators during imaging and data analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: The investigators were blinded during imaging and data analysis.
source: Strengths of this study were its prospective design and the blinding of the investigators during imaging and data analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: PD patients were clinically well-characterized, allowing search for correlations of cellular physiological and clinical parameters.
source: PD patients were clinically well-characterized, allowing us to search for correlations of cellular physiological and clinical parameters.
evidence: This is a description of the study design strength.

claim: Cohabitation results in overlapping gut microbiome profiles.
source: This is important in the light of recent data showing that cohabitation results in overlapping gut microbiome profiles (Yatsunenko et al., 2012) and that the composition of the gut microbiome may be related to the clinical manifestations of PD (Scheperjans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yatsunenko et al., 2012.

claim: The composition of the gut microbiome may be related to the clinical manifestations of PD.
source: This is important in the light of recent data showing that cohabitation results in overlapping gut microbiome profiles (Yatsunenko et al., 2012) and that the composition of the gut microbiome may be related to the clinical manifestations of PD (Scheperjans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scheperjans et al., 2015.

claim: The number of subjects in the study was relatively small.
source: Our study also has some limitations. The number of subjects was relatively small.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: Patients with young-onset PD were somewhat overrepresented in the study.
source: Patients with young-onset PD were somewhat overrepresented, possibly reflecting the greater willingness of young PD patients to participate in a demanding study.
evidence: This is an observation about the study population with a speculative explanation.

claim: The PD and control groups were not gender-matched.
source: Another limitation was that the PD and control groups were not gender-matched.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The lack of gender matching was a consequence of the pairwise recruitment in combination with the fact that the majority of PD participants were male.
source: This was a consequence of the pairwise recruitment in combination with the fact that the majority of PD participants, as in most clinical PD studies, were male.
evidence: This is an explanation for the gender imbalance in the study.

claim: Using the same calcium imaging technology, alterations in submucous neurons were previously found in functional dyspepsia patients.
source: Nevertheless, using the same technology, we previously found alterations in submucous neurons in functional dyspepsia patients (Cirillo et al., 2015), demonstrating the robustness of the techniques to detect changes, even subtle, in disease conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cirillo et al., 2015.

claim: The calcium and mitochondrial imaging assays are robust enough to detect changes, even subtle, in disease conditions.
source: Nevertheless, using the same technology, we previously found alterations in submucous neurons in functional dyspepsia patients (Cirillo et al., 2015), demonstrating the robustness of the techniques to detect changes, even subtle, in disease conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous successful application of the techniques.

claim: The study was unable to sample and analyze myenteric neurons due to safety reasons.
source: Another limitation is that we were unable to sample and analyze myenteric neurons due to safety reasons, as discussed above.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The duodenum was chosen as the sampling site based on evidence that α-synuclein aggregation in the ENS in PD is deposited with a rostrocaudal gradient.
source: It is also possible that the duodenum was not the optimal site for detection of neuronal changes in PD. However, we precisely chose a proximal GI site based on evidence that α-synuclein aggregation in the ENS in PD is deposited with a rostrocaudal gradient (Visanji et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a rationale for the choice of sampling site supported by citation to Visanji et al., 2014.

claim: Proximal portions of the GI tract receive stronger vagal innervation than distal regions.
source: Moreover, proximal portions of the GI tract receive stronger vagal innervation than distal regions (Ruffmann and Parkkinen, 2016) which, in view of the hypothesis that the vagus nerve transmits PD pathology, makes this region especially interesting.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruffmann and Parkkinen, 2016.

claim: Duodenal endoscopy is better tolerated and requires less demanding patient preparation compared to colonoscopy.
source: Also, duodenal endoscopy is better tolerated and requires less demanding patient preparation compared to colonoscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantages of duodenal endoscopy.

claim: The study cannot exclude the possibility that the duodenal submucosal plexus in PD patients is affected in a non-uniform, 'patchy' fashion and that affected ganglia were missed due to spatial sampling error.
source: Finally, we cannot exclude the possibility that the duodenal submucosal plexus in PD patients is affected in a non-uniform, 'patchy' fashion and that we missed affected ganglia due to spatial sampling error.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential study limitation.

claim: The findings suggest that GI symptoms in PD do not arise from dysfunction of submucous neurons.
source: In conclusion, we have applied live imaging techniques to investigate neuronal physiology in primary neurons from PD patients. Our findings suggest that GI symptoms in PD do not arise from dysfunction of submucous neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The data do not support the theory that the disease process of PD initiates in the submucous layers of the ENS and spreads from there to the brain.
source: Furthermore, our data do not support the theory that the disease process of PD initiates in the submucous layers of the ENS and spreads from there to the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Inclusion criterion for PD patients was diagnosis of PD according to the Gelb criteria.
source: Inclusion criterion for PD patients was diagnosis of PD according to the Gelb criteria (Gelb et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a description of the study inclusion criteria supported by citation to Gelb et al., 1999.

claim: GI symptoms were not a requirement for inclusion of PD patients.
source: GI symptoms were not a requirement for inclusion.
evidence: This is a description of the study inclusion criteria.

claim: An experienced endoscopist obtained 8 biopsies from the second part of the duodenum from each PD patient and control.
source: An experienced endoscopist at the Gastroenterology unit of the University Hospitals Leuven obtained 8 biopsies from the second part of the duodenum from each PD patient and control.
evidence: This is a description of the study procedure.

claim: Each pair of PD patient and control underwent endoscopy on the same day immediately one after another in random order.
source: Each pair underwent endoscopy on the same day immediately one after another in random order.
evidence: This is a description of the study procedure.

claim: All subjects had a macroscopically normal upper GI tract, except for one control with minor reflux esophagitis.
source: All subjects had a macroscopically normal upper GI tract, except for one control with minor reflux esophagitis.
evidence: This is a description of the endoscopic findings.

claim: All tissue manipulations, experiments and data analyses were performed by investigators blinded to the disease status of the subject.
source: The duodenal biopsies were immediately immersed in oxygenated ice-cold Krebs solution (in mM: 120.9 NaCl, 5.9 KCl, 1.2 MgCl2, 2.5 CaCl2, 11.5 glucose, 14.4 NaHCO3, and 1.2 NaH2PO4) and coded. All subsequent tissue manipulations, experiments and data analyses were performed by investigators blinded to the disease status (PD versus control) of the subject.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology to ensure unbiased analysis.

claim: Fast excitatory transmission in the ENS occurs mainly via acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors.
source: In addition to high K+ depolarization we also used two more physiological stimuli to assess neuronal function: 1,1-dimethyl-4-phenylpiperazinium (DMPP), a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist, as fast excitatory transmission in the ENS occurs mainly via acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors; and trains of electrical pulses applied to the fiber strands in the submucous plexus.

evidence: This is a rationale for the methodological approach.

claim: The complete destaining of TMRE in the presence of FCCP indicates that TMRE specifically labeled mitochondria.
source: To test whether TMRE specifically labelled mitochondria, we used carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylhydrazone (FCCP, 3 μM), a protonophore that quickly dissipates mitochondrial membrane potential. The complete destaining indicates that TMRE specifically labeled mitochondria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the TMRE labeling specificity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
